cs.t: The machine I'm typing this on is a 'whitebox' build I put together in 2010. I build computers to last - the specs were high-end at the time, and have been upgraded over the years (video card, RAID controller, SSD's, etc).  Even though it's getting long in the tooth, the box is still reasonably performant today. It's highly customized; the case sports thoughtful additions like sound-dampening foam, bespoke brackets for additional cooling fans (all Noctua of course), hardware thermostats & monitoring LCD, interior lighting that activates when you open a panel even if the machine is off (makes it a pleasure to work with when under a desk), etc. Choices that really panned out well include: Infiniband (this was back when 10G NIC's were stupid-expensive, but eBay was flooded with great, second-hand Mellanox cards off universities), Areca (their RAID controllers and arrays were so easily upgradeable across generations), ECC RAM everywhere, and an external PCI-E expander (six x16 slots just weren't enough). It has in the range of 1000 software titles installed, countless ones used regularly (guess I'm somewhat a jack of all trades).  Specialized diagnostics and tooling track and isolate changes made by software, which has helped manage things and prevent bloat accretion.  I periodically run benchmarks to ensure metrics like bootup time, disk transfers, etc. still match out-of-the-box numbers). When you have to install and configure that many apps, migration is a real pain, which mot…

cs.t: Every other brans of fans I have used (which to be fair is far from all of them) have only lasted 3 maybe 4 years before they started making more noise than when new. They weren't completely broken, but any increase in noise is unacceptable to me. I live in an old quiet house, there is no noise from forced ventilation but because it doesn't have that. There is no city noise. On a still day in the winter with no wind or birdsong it can be extremely quiet. I have some Noctua fans still going strong after a decade. Are there other brands that can also do that? Probably, I have some BeQuiet fans now too in a tower CPU cooler (couldn't get hold of a Noctua cooler during the pandemic), it will be interesting to see what happens in another 6 years or so with them. And no, I don't change my computer every 3 years or so any more, so longevity does matter to me.

cs.t: I am sure that they are overpriced, but the reason is because they can get away with this. Despite the fact that I think that it is very likely that a $40 cooler like the one mentioned by you would work well enough, when I will build a new computer with a top model AMD Ryzen CPU, which dissipates up to 200 W in steady state conditions, I will certainly buy a Noctua cooler for it. A computer with an Intel Arrow Lake S CPU would be even more demanding, as those can dissipate much more than 250 W in steady state conditions. The reason is that by now I have the experience with many Noctua coolers that have been working for 10 years or more, even 24/7, with perfect reliability and ensuring low noise and low temperatures. I am not willing to take the risk of experimenting with a replacement, so for my peace of mind I prefer the proven solutions, both for coolers and for power supply units (for the latter I use Seasonic). Noctua knows that many customers think like this, so they charge accordingly.

cs.t: Airflow is typically measured for worst-case scenarios or not measured at all but just something pulled off a datasheet and then they install the cheapest fan they can find that meets the specs. My SOP is to open the case, get thermal readings, drop in a Noctua, and keep dropping the voltage while taking thermal readings to make sure nothing is getting too hot. I've got an NVR where I've dropped the speed to the lowest at which it will still start and it's still blowing cold air through the vents, so the 40mm screamer that was there initially was total overkill. You can also get non-Noctua hydrodynamic bearing fans with polycarbonate blades and silicone mounts which are supposed to be very quiet, but I've never compared one against a Noctua. Anyone done a comparison?

cs.t: I never understood why so many devices were using such poor quality and noisy fans. They fail earlier, they move less air and they're noisier. Now I understand there's a cost issue, but it's not only that: a lot of it is also just poor design / poor research / poor parts sourcing. For the little story, back in the early beige PC days (think 386 and 486), quiet PC fans didn't exist. It was all super noisy, and typically at a fixed speed. And, coming from the Commodore 64 and then Commodore Amiga that were silent machines, this was driving me crazy. So 18 y/o me managed to source some proper fans out of Japan (Panaflo fans IIRC)  and  I went bug my neighbor, who was studying to become a chip engineer... I came to my neighbor with an idea:  "Why not lower the fan speed when the PC ain't too warm and then only speed it up when the PC gets too warm, you know, like a car's fan adapts to temperature?"  (cars would do that: they'd start spinning a huge fan to cool down the water in the car's radiator, but only once the water would be too warm). And so my neighbor drew a little electronical circuit and we bought "thermistors": I would "calibrate" them with boiling water in my mom's kitchen and then we'd install the circuit with the thermistor in the PC's PSU, with Panaflo fans. So basically: back in the 386 and then 486 days, I already had quiet PCs. cs.t: One issue I've had with swapping fans for Noctuas is the airflow matching. The louder fans aren't louder just because they're lower quality (which they definitely are), but also because (almost always in my experience) they force more air through. That unit from the article sounds very temperature sensitive. I'd be wary of throwing a precision unit like that out of spec and out of calibration. FWIW I've noctua-swapped so many things including an oscilloscope.

cs.t: If we're going by anecdotes, my last Noctuas showing signs of failure (I had 6 of them, one was ~200rpm slower than it should be, one took a several seconds longer to start spinning from a stop) about a year after the end of warranty was why I retired them. I suppose they all technically still spun so they were still usable, just not to original performance; still, hard to be too upset about the product making it through the long warranty period without issue. But my Arctics that was installed in the same case that ran for the same amount of time are still chugging along strong, and those are about as cheap as fans get. Different load/use case though so it's probably not a fair comparison. These days, I really think the competition has caught up or passed Noctua.

cs.t: I used to really like Noctua fans, for a while they were obviously the best fans by a significant margin. But for all their tight tolerances and exotic materials and a high price to match, they generally don't outperform BeQuiet's more regular materials but use-focused fans that are half the price. Nor are they significantly better than Arctic's general purpose fans at a quarter the price. Seems like it'd make more sense to just buy the fan optimized for the specific common purpose (airflow or radiator) than pay double for the Noctua for a more generalized fan, but is not the best at either common use case. Seems like these days their target audience is those who believe their marketing materials about them being the best, instead of believing the benchmark performance data.
cs.th: Why does it take so long to release black fan versions?

cs.t: In my experience fans from manufacturers like Arctic can be almost as quiet similar Noctua, but cost 50% less. The difference definitely isn't vast for most models, although admittedly there's more QC issues and variation than with Noctua. A lot of Noctua sales come from their brand value. People put Noctua fans into their gaming PC's, use headphones while gaming on them, and then turn off the PC. You don't really need the most silent fan for that, but people buy them anyway for the looks & premium quality. I do love Noctua's coolers though, I appreciate the well thought design, manuals and free upgrade kits when you upgrade your system to a new socket type. But for case fans I'll jut buy Arctic and save money, except for things like server systems that run 24/7 in my bedroom where noise and durability are top priority.
